verdict.rationale: Linear's first-party Loops let users describe a job in plain language and run it on a schedule or in response to workspace events, such as a project target-date change. That is a native trigger-and-action automation, but the action is an AI-agent workflow, not a configurable deterministic rule, and the depth of available triggers and actions is only sketched. An older community comment calls workflow automation Linear's biggest weakness, but it predates Loops, so it is not a concrete contradiction; webhooks and the API are developer building blocks and earn no credit. Missing for 10: a documented rule builder with explicit trigger/condition/action configuration, a catalog of supported triggers and actions, and independent hands-on corroboration of Loops.

support.subject: As an engineer, I can build trigger-and-action automation rules to eliminate repetitive manual steps

citations.quote: Loops are a new way for Linear Agent to take on recurring work for your team. Describe the job in plain language and then choose whether it should run on a schedule or in response to an event.
They now respond to more workspace activity, including changes to initiatives, projects, and cycles.
When a project's target date changes, a loop can automatically update the launch plan and post a Slack message explaining what changed, why, and who needs to act.
